The History of a Small Diagram

In the beginning there was only a sketch on the back of an envelope. The team
had been working on the new payment system for several months, and nobody
could remember which service talked to which. One morning, the architect took
a pencil and drew three boxes, a few arrows and a question mark. "This is what
we have," she said, "and this is what we need to understand before the next
release." The developers looked at the drawing for a long time. Some of them
nodded; others were not convinced at all.

During the following weeks the envelope travelled from desk to desk. Every
person who received it added something: a database here, a queue there, a
comment in the margin about the security of the connection between the web
server and the internal network. By the end of the month the drawing was
almost impossible to read. The arrows crossed each other, the boxes overlapped,
and the original question mark had disappeared under a cloud of corrections.

That is when somebody suggested writing the diagram as text. "If the picture
is generated from a description," he explained, "then everyone can change it,
review it and keep it in the repository with the rest of the code." The idea
was simple, but it changed the way the team worked. Instead of arguing about
the position of a box, people discussed the relationships between components.
Instead of redrawing everything after each change, they edited a single line
and generated a new image in less than a second.

IMPORTANT: The description must remain readable. A diagram that nobody can
maintain is worse than no diagram at all. Keep the names short, group related
elements in packages, and add a title that explains the purpose of the view.

Today the payment system has grown into a large platform with dozens of
services. The original envelope is framed on the wall of the meeting room,
next to a printed copy of the current architecture. Visitors often ask which
one is more useful. The answer is always the same: the first one started the
conversation, and the second one keeps it going. Both of them are important,
because a good diagram is not only a picture of a system; it is also a record
of the decisions that shaped it, the questions that were asked, and the people
who took the time to answer them.

Questions? Comments? Please contact the Documentation Team. We are happy to
help you with your first diagram, your hundredth diagram, or anything else
related to the documentation of our software.
